analysis.title: Wargaming The AI Crash (Macro Picture)
key_insights: TS Lombard models an AI-bust scenario: US stocks fall at least 30% (about $20 trillion of market cap), credit spreads widen and tech-related defaults follow. They expect only a mild US recession, comparable to 1990 and 2001.
Their working assumption is that the AI capex boom ends in early 2028, but the date could slip. Shorting US tech or adding duration too early would underperform.
The boom is still largely capex recycling and circular financing. Their sustainability metric, the ratio of internal to external ecosystem revenues, is little changed since their June note.
US tech companies invest around $1 trillion a year in the AI buildout. Studies put the revenue hurdle rate at $2.5-3.0 trillion by 2030, about 14 times today's revenue.
Open-weight Chinese models are gaining share and consumers are reluctant to pay. About 80% of OpenAI and Anthropic revenue comes from 1% of customers, mostly unprofitable AI startups.

Debt is now the marginal source of AI funding. AI companies are expected to issue about $700 billion of bonds in 2027, $400 billion of it from hyperscalers, more than all euro-area governments combined.

Off-balance-sheet structures hide liabilities. Meta's $30 billion Hyperion data center was 80% sold to Brown Owl, and the resulting JV Beignet raised $27 billion of debt backed by a 20-year Meta leaseback. Hidden liabilities across the ecosystem are estimated at $1.5-2 trillion.
Borrowing costs are rising: the Fed is hiking, yields are rising and junk spreads are widening. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave already pay about 15% interest.

Teaser-rate and accounting issues: depreciation only starts when data centers enter service, and lab lease commitments only start once the capacity is live. Both flatter balance sheets today and will weigh later.

Anthropic and OpenAI IPOs are planned, though OpenAI's has been pushed to 2027. IPO waves often mark cycle tops, and lockup expiries let insiders sell. The filings would also reveal the true economics.

NVIDIA is the barometer of the boom. It engages in vendor financing, and a BIS study finds over 55% of incoming AI-firm investment comes from other AI firms. Double-ordering of hardware could turn shortages into a glut if demand slows.

Regulatory backlash is a risk: about 55% of Americans want AI development to slow versus 13% who don't. A serious AI-enabled attack could trigger a crackdown, especially if US politics turns less tech-friendly after the midterms.

The second-derivative problem: capex does not need to fall to cause stress, it only needs to grow more slowly. The financing resembles a loan book in which frontier-lab contracts are the debt service and the data center is the collateral.

Tech is about 40% of US market cap and semiconductors nearly 20%. Trailing tech P/E is about 30, down from 40 a year ago and below the 70-75 Dotcom peak. The base case is S&P 500 -30%, tech -40%, other sectors -20%.

Credit: hyperscalers will have issued about $780 billion of debt by the end of the boom and are not seen as serious credit risks. Strain would hit neoclouds, project vehicles, Oracle, standalone model developers and AI app startups.

Total AI debt is about $2.9 trillion, with roughly 25% considered vulnerable. Applying a 35% cumulative default rate over 2028-30 and 25-50% recovery gives losses of $125-190 billion, which is material but not systemic. The closer analogy is the late-1980s S&L episode.

Economy: the AI crash would cut about 2 percentage points from the level of US GDP, partly offset by lower imports. Data-center jobs of about 500k, rising to 800k, would add about 50bps to unemployment if lost.
Wealth effects are weak: the link between wealth and the savings rate broke down after 2016, because equity wealth is concentrated among high earners with low marginal propensity to consume.

A mild recession is expected because private balance sheets are healthy, monetary ammo is abundant, and rate cuts would revive the bottom of the K-shaped economy. They suggest a new housing bubble could follow, as it did after Dotcom.
Downside risks to the mild baseline are a confidence shock, reflexive job losses, and a cyclical-downturn-driven wave of AI automation leading to a jobless recovery.
Government bonds: an AI crash is a demand shock, unlike the 1970s supply shocks, so yields would fall and the bond-equity correlation would turn negative. They do not expect a return to ZIRP or QE.

Rest of world: Korea and Taiwan are heavily exposed, with tech exports adding 10-30% of GDP. Other markets have low exposure, and non-AI, non-US stocks should outperform over time despite an initial indiscriminate sell-off.
Dollar: they expect the dollar to fall in an AI crash, unlike in 2008. Funds would shift to the euro, yen and perhaps sterling, since global investors can use domestic bonds as safe havens.

Positioning: they favor a diversified portfolio of global stocks at a normal level of risk, citing GMO's Ben Inker on 'hard' vs 'easy' bubbles. Duration should be added over time as stress appears in riskier parts of the AI ecosystem.

sector_views.rationale: An AI crash would hit US tech hardest, with tech stocks assumed down 40% and earnings falling with recycled capex.

sector_views.sector: Semiconductors and AI supply chain (Korea, Taiwan)
sector_views.rationale: Highly exposed to a capex slowdown, with tech exports adding 10-30% of GDP in Korea and Taiwan.
Low AI exposure, so they would outperform over time and benefit from lower global yields.
Yields fall in a demand-driven downturn, but duration should be added only once AI stress emerges.

earnings_insights: Hyperscaler earnings are largely capex recycling. Revenues would be downgraded in a crash, with a hit to the 'other' revenue category, which is valuation gains on crossholdings in other AI companies.

macro_indicators.reading: about -2 percentage points on the level of GDP

macro_indicators.interpretation: Equities are a concentrated AI bet, so a bust hits indices hard.

trade_ideas.description: Hold a diversified portfolio of global equities rather than US tech-concentrated exposure
trade_ideas.rationale: It keeps a normal amount of risk, does well if the boom continues and should outperform in a crash.
trade_ideas.risk: Initial indiscriminate sell-off in all equities in a crash.

trade_ideas.description: Add government bond duration gradually as signs of stress appear in riskier parts of the AI ecosystem
trade_ideas.rationale: In an AI-driven demand shock, yields would fall and bonds would hedge equities.
trade_ideas.risk: Adding duration too early underperforms while yields keep rising.

trade_ideas.description: Short the US dollar, expressed against the euro, yen and perhaps sterling
trade_ideas.rationale: Destruction centered on US financial system pushes funds to other jurisdictions.
trade_ideas.risk: Dollar safe-haven bid as in the 2008 crisis.

risk_factors: AI revenues falling short of the $2.5-3.0 trillion hurdle rate
Debt-funded capex with rising rates and wider junk spreads
Off-balance-sheet liabilities of $1.5-2 trillion and opaque financing
Depreciation cliff and lab lease commitments starting when data centers go live
Vendor financing and circular funding in the AI ecosystem
Public opposition and regulatory backlash after a serious AI incident
IPO lockup expiries and insider selling
Reflexive job losses and AI automation in a downturn
charts_described: Chart 12: tech share of US stock market rose to about 40%.
Chart 13: semiconductors and related equipment near 20% of US market cap.

Chart 28: Korea and Taiwan tech exports as a share of GDP are shown as heavily exposed, with exports adding 10-30% of GDP.
vol_and_positioning: Clients are mostly fully invested in risk assets and nobody is shorting US tech or betting on an immediate crash.
Markets have been jittery in recent weeks.
The report advises against shorting tech or adding duration too early. It favors a diversified global equity portfolio and adding bonds as AI strain emerges.
geopolitical: Chinese open-weight AI models are gaining share, raising commoditization risk for US AI.
US midterms: politics may turn less tech-friendly afterward, raising regulatory risk.
The report mentions an energy crisis that, when it ends, would help diversified global stocks.
cross_bank_references: Agrees with GMO's Ben Inker on diversified global stocks for trading hard vs easy bubbles
Disagrees with Julien Garran's claim that the AI buildout is the 'biggest misallocation of capital in history'
IMF's latest WEO estimates are 'remarkably similar' to TS Lombard's GDP impact estimate

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings keep rising, the tech P/E of about 30 is below the Dotcom peak of 70-75, and clients see frontier AI as good enough to matter.
tension_points.bear_case: Revenue is mostly recycled capex and circular financing, the $2.5-3.0 trillion hurdle rate is about 14 times current revenue, and debt is now the marginal funding source.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A slowdown in the growth rate of hyperscaler capex (the second-derivative problem), or NVIDIA disappointing expectations.

tension_points.bull_case: Only a mild recession: balance sheets are healthy, the Fed has room to cut, rate cuts revive the bottom of the K-shaped economy, and credit losses are not systemic.
tension_points.bear_case: A confidence shock, reflexive job losses and AI-driven automation in the downturn could produce a worse, jobless recovery.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Employment starting to contract, triggering reflexive spending and profit declines.
